title: Configuration and Precedence knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Configuration and Precedence”?
options: Grouping commands in the current shell
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Defaults in scripts” under lesson 83, “Configuration and Precedence”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Configuration and Precedence”?
options: Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics.
questions.explanation: Validate inputs, define usage, and keep machine-readable output separate from diagnostics. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Configuration and Precedence”?
options: Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
questions.answer_key: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
questions.explanation: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
